rules.rule: Start by distinguishing primary, secondary, and tertiary aging exactly instead of saying aging just gets worse overall.
rules.reason: The professor repeatedly brought the discussion back to that three-part distinction and used it as the main organizing frame for the chapter.

rules.rule: When you mention a visible bodily change, connect it immediately to mechanism, daily-life function, or autonomy.
rules.reason: The professor explicitly endorsed the reading that this chapter is about function and autonomy, not only outward appearance.

rules.rule: If you say something is preventable or manageable, place it under secondary aging and name the concrete factor such as sun exposure, noise exposure, inactivity, diet, smoking, or disease.
rules.reason: The class repeatedly used concrete examples to show what counts as modifiable secondary aging rather than unavoidable primary aging.

rules.rule: Use the exact technical term when it matters, especially REM sleep, testosterone, telomere, terminal decline, and time to death.
rules.reason: Several discussion points turned on specific terms, and imprecise wording would blur distinct concepts.

rules.rule: If you cite outside news or video material, label it as supplementary and explain the design limit before you draw a conclusion.
rules.reason: The professor stopped to note that the 34, 60, 78 article was a cross-sectional design and later marked the Hallmarks and Sinclair material as beyond the textbook.

rules.rule: If you say the chapter was interesting or surprising, explain what assumption changed, such as moving from an appearance-centered view of aging to a function-centered one.
rules.reason: The best student responses in this class did not stop at saying a topic was interesting; they stated what prior expectation changed.

rules.rule: When discussing life extension or anti-aging technology, add one concrete social consequence such as inequality, care burden, or lack of social preparation.
rules.reason: The professor opened a class discussion about unequal access and the social side of longevity rather than treating the technology as automatically good.
